title: Bounding Retraining Equivalence and the Deletion Floor in Materials Machine Unlearning
authors: Can Polat, Mustafa Kurban, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban
abstract: In materials machine learning, closely related retained structures can sustain accurate property predictions even after removing a specific record, rendering post-deletion prediction error an ambiguous metric for machine unlearning. To resolve this ambiguity, we define the deletion floor as the expected target loss under a specified retraining procedure at the deleted request. Standard indistinguishability constraints yield a sharp interval bounding an update's target loss around this baseline reference. Theoretically, a conditional neighbor bound links a low deletion floor directly to retained fit, prediction regularity, and local label agreement, while an exact ridge identity isolates residual fit from the prediction change induced by record deletion. Empirically, controlled redundancy sweeps show an $\approx 8\times$ drop in median normalized retraining loss when one retained relative remains after deletion. Across two distinct fitting regimes in a paired Materials Project study, the lower-floor regime also exhibits a larger prediction change on more than 50% of the shared requests. Systematic comparisons against approximate updates and the original model decouple deliberate target suppression from preserved overall model utility. Consequently, request-level unlearning evaluations should report reference loss, prediction change, and retained utility together, interpreting post-deletion accuracy against what retraining itself leaves behind.
summary: This paper introduces the 'deletion floor' as a robust metric to quantify the expected residual error when performing machine unlearning on materials data. It develops theoretical tools to bound this error based on retraining equivalence and provides empirical evidence showing that structural redundancy significantly stabilizes predictions after data deletion. This shifts the focus of unlearning evaluation from simple post-deletion accuracy to a comprehensive view of retained model utility.
main_problem: Standard metrics for machine unlearning in materials science are ambiguous because related retained data can maintain accurate predictions even after a record is deleted.
main_result: The authors propose the 'deletion floor' as the definitive metric, showing that unlearning evaluations must report reference loss, prediction change, and retained utility together.
method: The work develops theoretical bounds using retraining equivalence and employs exact ridge regression identities to calculate the deletion floor and residual fit.
model_or_system: The study applies to machine learning models trained on materials datasets, mapping crystal structures and compositions to target properties like formation energy.
key_observables: Deletion floor ($\Phi$), Prediction Change, Retained Utility, Loss Gap ($g_i$), and retraining loss.
important_parameters: The size of the retained relative set, the regularization parameter ($\lambda$), and the equivalence parameters ($\epsilon, \delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on strong convexity assumptions for theoretical bounds and assumes that the deletion floor resolves the ambiguity of post-deletion accuracy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that related materials can keep a removed record predictable, defining the deletion floor as the expected retraining loss, and show the drop in retraining loss when retained relatives remain.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the ambiguity in unlearning metrics to defining the deletion floor, deriving theoretical bounds using retraining equivalence, and validating these concepts using both synthetic and real-world materials datasets.
why_interesting: While focused on ML, the rigorous mathematical framework for bounding information retention and residual error after data removal shares conceptual parallels with understanding system stability or information leakage in complex quantum systems.
